# Do Explanations of Manipulation Policies Survive Dynamics Shift? Closed-Loop Faithfulness and Attribution-Shift Failure Prediction

*Draft technical report, Project V MVP. Every number in this document is generated by
`scripts/make_tables.py` from files in `results/`; `TBD` marks results not yet computed.*

## Summary

<!-- BEGIN:headline -->
- Held-out-dynamics (sim-to-sim) success on FetchPush, mean over n=1/2 seeds [95% bootstrap CI]: NoDR **34.9% (n=1, no seed CI)**, DR **23.1% [17.9, 28.3] (s0 6.2%, s1 40.0%)**.
- Failure prediction from the first 10 of 50 steps (push_dr, test split): ASM AUROC **0.713 [0.689, 0.737]** vs best baseline (q_drop) **0.744 [0.722, 0.765]**.
<!-- END:headline -->

## 1. Introduction

Robot policies trained in simulation are deployed under dynamics they did not see in training:
different friction, payload mass, controller response, sensor noise and latency. Two practical
questions follow for anyone who explains such policies with feature attributions. First, does an
explanation computed one state at a time (open loop) tell us what the policy actually depends on
when it acts over a whole episode (closed loop)? Second, when the dynamics shift, does the
explanation shift too, and does that shift warn us before the task fails?

We study these questions on simulated manipulation with SAC+HER policies on Gymnasium-Robotics
`FetchReach` and `FetchPush` (MuJoCo). The policies are trained under three conditions: no
dynamics randomization (NoDR), dynamics domain randomization (DR), and DR with a short history of
observations and actions (DR+Hist). All shifts are **held-out dynamics within the same
simulator (sim-to-sim)**. We make no claim about transfer to physical robots.

Contributions:

- **C1, closed-loop faithfulness with ground truth.** We score seven attribution methods against
  an analytic Cartesian PD controller, whose relevant inputs and exact contributions are known,
  and against a Reach policy trained with a planted shortcut feature. On learned Push policies we
  compare open-loop rankings (action-distribution divergence under erasure) with closed-loop
  importance (success drop when a group is erased at every step).
- **C2, GWIE-C.** We adapt GWIE, a gradient-guided iterative-erasure method from the DePlag
  plagiarism-explanation system, to continuous Gaussian policies over semantic feature groups.
  The adaptation and every deviation from the original are documented in
  `docs/gwie_original.md`, and a direct port is reported next to it.
- **C3, Attribution-Shift Monitor (ASM).** A Mahalanobis score on the per-step vector of group
  attribution shares, fit on nominal-dynamics calibration episodes, used to predict episode
  failure from the first 10 or 25 of 50 steps. It is compared with five baselines under identical
  smoothing and aggregation.
- **C4, what DR changes.** Group and temporal reliance profiles across conditions, and linear
  probes testing whether actor activations encode friction, mass and gain beyond what the raw
  inputs carry.

## 2. Related work

**Explaining robot-manipulation policies.** Kim and Choi (arXiv:2310.19432) explain the decisions
of deep policy networks for robotic manipulation. Dai, Arulkumaran et al. (arXiv:1912.08324)
analyse DRL agents trained with domain randomisation and inspect how randomisation changes what
the agents use, which C4 revisits with grouped attributions and probes.

**Faithfulness of saliency in RL.** Atrey, Clary and Jensen (ICLR 2020) argue that saliency maps
for RL agents are often exploratory rather than explanatory and call for counterfactual tests.
Huber et al. (Frontiers in AI, 2022) benchmark perturbation-based saliency for Atari agents.
AttributionLab (Zhang et al., arXiv:2310.06514) evaluates attributions where the ground truth is
known by construction, the idea behind our analytic-controller and planted-shortcut settings.
IMPACT-VLA (arXiv:2609.15005) studies closed-loop counterfactual attribution for
vision-language-action models. C1 asks the closed-loop question for low-dimensional state
policies, where analytic ground truth is available.

**Explanation shift and failure prediction.** Mougan et al. (arXiv:2303.08081) propose monitoring
shifts in explanations, rather than in inputs, to detect distribution shift that matters to the
model. Early-warning signals for OpenVLA failure under visual distribution shift
(arXiv:2606.29699) and RoboMD (Sagar et al., ICLR 2026, arXiv:2412.02818) address failure
discovery and prediction for robot policies. C3 tests an explanation-shift monitor under
*dynamics* shift and compares it with input-, uncertainty-, value- and activation-based baselines.

**Domain randomization and adaptation.** Active Domain Randomization (Mehta et al.,
arXiv:1904.04762) and DORAEMON (Tiboni et al., arXiv:2311.01885) adapt the randomization
distribution. Chen et al. (ICLR 2022, arXiv:2110.03239) analyse when DR transfers and why history
helps. RMA (Kumar et al., arXiv:2107.04034) adapts online from a history of states and actions,
the motivation for our DR+Hist condition and for the system-identification probes. XFD
(arXiv:2610.16478) uses XAI to guide domain generalisation for sim-to-real DRL.

**Tooling and statistics.** We follow Agarwal et al. (NeurIPS 2021, `rliable`) in reporting
bootstrap confidence intervals and per-seed values rather than point estimates. MuJoCo-based
manipulation suites such as the Franka environments of Xu et al. (arXiv:2312.13788) and MuJoCo
Playground (Zakka et al., arXiv:2502.08844) are natural next targets (out of scope here).

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Tasks, policies and dynamics

Fetch environments return a dictionary with `observation` (10-D for Reach, 25-D for Push),
`achieved_goal` and `desired_goal`. Actions are 4-D end-effector displacements plus a gripper
command, applied through mocap. Episodes last 50 steps, and success is `is_success` at the final
step. Policies are SAC+HER (SB3, `MultiInputPolicy`) with hyperparameters taken from the
rl-baselines3-zoo Fetch configurations. TQC+HER is the documented fallback if SAC does not learn.
SAC+HER learned Push in only 1 of 6 runs, so every reported Push policy is TQC+HER (same buffer and
HER settings). The first Push runs stopped at the Kaggle wall-clock cap after ~759k of the planned
1M steps; the later seeds were capped at 760k steps so that every Push seed has the same budget.

Dynamics factors are resampled at every reset in DR training: object sliding friction, table
friction, object mass, a control-gain multiplier, observation noise and action latency. Three
implementation details matter for interpreting the results:

- **Control gain** multiplies the mocap step size after the env's action clip. With mocap control,
  arm joint dynamics barely affect behaviour, so this factor stands in for "actuator gain" and
  should not be read as a joint-level actuator randomization.
- **Friction.** MuJoCo combines contact friction as the element-wise maximum of the two geoms, so
  scaling only the object would leave low-friction settings without effect against the table.
  Both the object and table geoms therefore receive the product of the two friction multipliers.
  A side effect is that gripper contacts get `max(1, product)`.
- **Observation noise** is added to `observation` and to the duplicated `achieved_goal` slice.

The held-out grid holds one-factor-at-a-time cells outside the training ranges plus random
combined cells. Its values were calibrated once on a DR policy so that success lies roughly in
20–80%, then frozen with a recorded hash. Every held-out result is computed on the frozen grid. The
Push grid was calibrated on push_dr seed 1, because seed 0 did not learn. Cells where no value
reached the band are kept and flagged, not dropped.

### 3.2 Attribution methods

All methods explain the pre-tanh action mean `mu(s)` over a flat state in raw units, aggregated to
semantic groups (`ee_pos`, `obj_pos`, `obj_rel`, `grip_state`, `obj_rot`, `obj_velp`,
`obj_velr`, `ee_vel`, `grip_vel`, `goal`). `achieved_goal` is grouped with the observation slice
it duplicates. Gradient methods differentiate the scalar `f(s') = <mu(s'), mu(s)/||mu(s)||>`, the
projection on the current action direction, because a divergence at `s' = s` has zero gradient.
Erasure replaces a group with values resampled from a calibration pool of states (8 samples,
averaged); zero baselines are never used for positions. Methods: gradient, gradient×delta,
integrated gradients (16 steps, pool-mean baseline), SmoothGrad, group occlusion, grouped
KernelSHAP, GWIE-C and the GWIE port.

### 3.3 GWIE-C

GWIE-C is adapted from GWIE (DePlag); deviations are listed in `docs/gwie_original.md`. The
original is a counterfactual-set search: it repeatedly computes integrated gradients of a
similarity score on the partially erased input, erases the highest-magnitude unit, and stops
once the similarity drops below a threshold. GWIE-C keeps the guided loop (IG recomputed on the
current erased state, magnitude pivot). It differs in three ways: it erases feature groups by
marginal resampling, runs until every group is erased, and assigns each group its marginal gain
in `KL(π(·|s) || π(·|s_erased))`. This yields a full ranking and a score for every group, which C1
needs. We checked the original empirically before porting it. It beats random erasure and comes
close to a brute-force greedy oracle, but the erasure trajectory is not monotone in general, and
we claim no monotonicity or convergence property for either variant.

### 3.4 Faithfulness protocol (C1)

*Ground truth A:* the analytic PD controller `mu = Kp (goal − ee_pos) − Kd ee_vel`, run in both
the Reach and the Push env, where all object groups are irrelevant. We report precision@k of the
relevant groups, Spearman ρ against the exact group contributions, and the share on irrelevant
groups. *Ground truth B:* a Reach policy trained with a hint feature equal to the noisy goal. At
test time the hint is intact or replaced by a random point. The success drop measures true
reliance, and methods are scored on the share they give the hint. *Learned Push policies:*
open-loop importance is the mean KL under group erasure. Closed-loop importance is the success
drop when a group is erased at every step of an episode, and also for the redundant cluster
`{ee_pos, obj_pos, obj_rel}`. Deletion curves erase the top-k groups of each method's ranking in
closed loop.

### 3.5 Attribution-Shift Monitor (C3)

At each step, `z_t` is the vector of IG group shares. A Ledoit–Wolf Gaussian fit on
nominal-dynamics calibration episodes gives `m_t = Mahalanobis(z_t)`, which is smoothed by an
EWMA. The prefix score is `max_{t≤T} e_t` for T ∈ {10, 25}. The baselines (`obs_ood`, `act_std`,
`q_drop`, `ensemble`, `act_ood`) use the same smoothing and aggregation. Each policy's rollouts
are split into calib and test by episode seed. α and the alarm threshold (5% false-positive rate
on calib successes) are chosen on calib, and all metrics are reported on test with a cluster
bootstrap that resamples seeds and then episodes.

### 3.6 Reliance and probes (C4)

Group shares (IG and GWIE-C) on nominal states per condition; for DR+Hist, shares on the time
slots t … t−3 and on past actions, nominal versus held-out. Ridge probes (5-fold CV over episodes)
predict log friction, log mass and gain from actor penultimate activations. The controls are
probes on the raw single-step observation, on the raw stacked observation (DR+Hist), and on a
randomly initialised actor.

### 3.7 Statistics

Training seeds: {0, 1, 2} for Reach. Push: push_dr seeds {0, 1, 2}, push_nodr and push_drhist
seeds {0, 1} (fallback step 4 of the plan, applied because the Kaggle GPU budget could not cover
9 runs × 1M steps). push_dr seed 0 did not learn (nominal success ~5%). It appears in the
robustness table with its per-seed value and is left out of C1, C3 and C4, which analyse learned
policies. Push is therefore two learned seeds per condition. With n = 2, CIs across seeds are
coarse, and the per-seed values should be read. The C3 `ensemble` baseline uses the two learned
seeds of each condition. Success per (policy, cell) averages at least 100 episodes.
Across seeds we report the mean with a 95% stratified bootstrap CI (2,000 resamples), always
alongside per-seed values. With n ≤ 3, IQM is degenerate and is not used.

The controller is linear, so gradient×delta and IG are exact by construction. This setting
verifies implementations and grouping, not faithfulness on learned non-linear policies.
`gwie_orig_port` stops at its similarity threshold and gives never-erased groups score 0, so its
ranking metrics are limited by design.

*Reading (push_dr seed 1, the only learned push_dr seed).* Occlusion and gradient × Δ agree most
with the closed-loop ranking. IG, KernelSHAP and both GWIE variants tie behind them and recover the
same top-k groups. Plain gradients and SmoothGrad agree least and miss most of the top-k groups that
closed-loop erasure identifies. GWIE-C's closed-loop agreement matches IG's, at a higher cost (Section
4.4). With one seed, method rankings that differ by less than the CI width should not be read as
differences.

*Reading.* From the first 10 steps, ASM's AUROC lies within the CIs of the best baseline for all
three Push policies. It is not clearly better or worse. The best baseline differs by condition
(`q_drop` for DR and DR+Hist, `obs_ood` for NoDR). From the first 25 steps, the critic-based `q_drop`
baseline is clearly best in all three conditions (CIs disjoint from ASM's). On this evidence ASM is
a competitive early signal on Push but does not beat a simple value-based monitor once more of the
episode is seen. Each Push condition is one training seed, so these comparisons cover episode-level
uncertainty only.

*Reading.* On nominal states the three Push policies put most attribution on the object–gripper
relation, the goal and the object position. The DR+Hist policy spreads part of its attribution over
the history slots and past actions, while the current step keeps the largest single share. That
temporal profile changes little between nominal and held-out cells. The probe claim rule is not met
for any (condition, target), so no implicit system identification is claimed for Push.

*Reading.* DR+Hist has the highest held-out success of the three Push conditions. The learned
push_dr seed is above NoDR on held-out dynamics, but the failed push_dr seed pulls the DR mean below
NoDR. With one learned seed per condition, this table cannot separate the effect of DR from
seed-to-seed variation in Push training. The three-seed Reach track (Section 4.8) is the better
evidence for the effect of DR.

### 4.8 Reach track (Gate G2 insurance)

Under Gate G2 (`mvp.md` §10), C3, C4 and the robustness evaluation were also run on FetchReach
with DR on control gain, observation noise and latency, the factors that affect Reach. Reach uses
its own frozen held-out grid (`configs/dr/heldout_reach.yaml`), calibrated on reach_dr seed 0.
It complements the Push results in Sections 4.3 and 4.5–4.7 (two learned seeds per condition)
with three seeds per condition.
All shifts are held-out dynamics within one simulator (sim-to-sim).

## 5. Limitations

- **Sim-to-sim only.** Held-out dynamics differ in friction, mass, mocap step size, noise and
  latency within one simulator. These results say nothing about transfer to a physical robot.
- **Few Push seeds.** Two learned seeds per Push condition (push_dr: two of three trained seeds
  learned). Conclusions may not generalise across seeds. Reach has three seeds per condition.
  Per-seed values are reported throughout and should be read.
- **Shortened training.** Push policies were trained for ~760k of the planned 1M steps.
- **Narrow setting.** One robot with mocap control, two tasks and one algorithm family. The
  "gain" factor is a mocap step-size multiplier, not an actuator randomization, and the friction
  factor also changes gripper contacts above nominal (Section 3.1).
- **Ground truth is easy for gradients.** The analytic controller is linear. The planted shortcut
  provides a non-linear ground truth for only one feature.
- **Calibrated grid.** Held-out values were chosen once so that one DR policy succeeds 20–80%
  of the time. The grid is therefore tied to that policy and is not a neutral sample of shifts.
- **GWIE lineage.** GWIE-C shares the original's guided-erasure mechanism but changes the target,
  the erasure operator, the stopping rule and the output (see `docs/gwie_original.md`). It should
  be read as an adaptation, not as the original method.
